To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“Firms decrease dividend payments after an exogenous shock that reduces information asymmetry between managers and investors, and that the information content (signaling) of dividends decreases in the post-shock period.
“Dividend payouts decrease after an improvement in the public information about firms’ investment decisions, but increase after an improvement in investors’ ability to extract cash dividends.
We examine the effects of an exogenous shock on the information asymmetry between managers and investors, and find that firms reduce dividend payouts, but increase dividend cuts, following the event.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of changes in information asymmetries on the payout policy of firms, and we provide evidence that firms adjust their dividend payouts in response to changes in their information environment.
the impact of changes in corporate information asymmetries on firms’ payout policies.
the role of information for corporate payout policy and governance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results are in line with agency theories, but that the effects are more pronounced in countries where agency costs are more important.
the agency theory of dividends is supported in a global setting.
the information environment is an important determinant of the dividend payout policy of firms, and that the effect is stronger when the agency issues are more pronounced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the information environment is an important determinant of the agency problem between investors and managers.
firms pay more dividends when the informational environment is less transparent, as it is the case in emerging markets.
the information content and the agency costs of dividends are not constant but vary with the information environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the agency problem is not only a static one but also a dynamic process, in which firms adapt their payout policies to changes in the information environment.
the information environment and the corporate governance structure have a significant impact on the dividend payout policy of firms.
the agency costs associated with free cash flow are a key driver of dividend policy.
